In [[geometry]], the [[incircle]] of the [[medial triangle]] of a triangle is the '''Spieker circle''', named after 19th-century German geometer [[Theodor Spieker]].<ref name=":05"/> Its center, the [[Spieker center]], in addition to being the [[incenter]] of the medial triangle, is the [[center of mass]] of the uniform-density boundary of triangle.<ref name=":05"/> The Spieker center is also the point where all three [[Cleaver (geometry)|cleaver]]s of the triangle (perimeter bisectors with an endpoint at a side's midpoint) intersect each other.<ref name=":05"/>

== History ==
The Spieker circle and Spieker center are named after [[Theodor Spieker]], a mathematician and professor from [[Potsdam]], Germany. In 1862, he published {{lang|de|Lehrbuch der ebenen geometrie mit übungsaufgaben für höhere lehranstalten}}, dealing with planar geometry. Due to this publication, influential in the lives of many famous scientists and mathematicians including [[Albert Einstein]], Spieker became the mathematician for whom the Spieker circle and center were named.<ref name=":05">{{Cite journal|last=de Villiers|first=Michael|date=June 2006|title=A generalisation of the Spieker circle and Nagel line|journal=Pythagoras|volume=63|pages=30–37}}</ref>

== Construction ==
To find the Spieker circle of a triangle, the [[medial triangle]] must first be constructed from the [[midpoint]]s of each side of the original triangle.<ref name=":05"/> The circle is then constructed in such a way that each side of the medial triangle is [[tangent]] to the circle within the medial triangle, creating the [[Incircle and excircles of a triangle|incircle]].<ref name=":05"/> This circle center is named the [[Spieker center]].

== Nagel points and lines ==
Spieker circles also have relations to [[Nagel point]]s. The [[incenter]] of the triangle and the Nagel point form a line within the Spieker circle. The middle of this line segment is the Spieker center.<ref name=":05"/> The Nagel line is formed by the incenter of the triangle, the Nagel point, and the [[centroid]] of the triangle.<ref name=":05"/> The Spieker center will always lie on this line.<ref name=":05"/>

== Nine-point circle and Euler line ==
Spieker circles were first found to be very similar to [[nine-point circle]]s by Julian Coolidge. At this time, it was not yet identified as the Spieker circle, but is referred to as the "P circle" throughout the book.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|title=A treatise on the circle and the sphere|title-link=A Treatise on the Circle and the Sphere|last=Coolidge|first=Julian L.|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=1916|pages=53–57}}</ref> The nine-point circle with the [[Euler line]] and the Spieker circle with the Nagel line are analogous to each other, but are not [[Duality (mathematics)|duals]], only having dual-like similarities.<ref name=":05"/> One similarity between the nine-point circle and the Spieker circle deals with their construction. The nine-point circle is the [[Circumscribed circle|circumscribed]] circle of the medial triangle, while the Spieker circle is the [[Inscribed circle|inscribed]] circle of the medial triangle.<ref name=":2" /> With relation to their associated lines, the incenter for the Nagel line relates to the circumcenter for the Euler line.<ref name=":05"/> Another analogous pair of points is the Nagel point and the [[orthocenter]], with the Nagel point associated with the Spieker circle and the orthocenter associated with the nine-point circle.<ref name=":05"/> In the first case, the [[Splitter (geometry)|splitters]] of the reference triangle, which pass through the Nagel point, also pass through the tangencies of the Spieker circle with the sides of medial triangle. In the second case, the [[Altitude (triangle)|altitudes]] of the reference triangle, which pass through the orthocenter, also pass through the intersections of the nine-point circle with the sides of the reference triangle.<ref name=":2" />

=== Spieker conic ===
The nine-point circle with the Euler line was generalized into the nine-point conic.<ref name=":05"/> Through a similar process, due to the analogous properties of the two circles, the Spieker circle was also able to be generalized into the Spieker conic.<ref name=":05" /> The Spieker conic is still found within the medial triangle and touches each side of the medial triangle, however it does not meet those sides of the triangle at the same points. If lines are constructed from each vertex of the medial triangle to the Nagel point, then the midpoint of each of those lines can be found.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://dynamicmathematicslearning.com/spiekernagelgeneral.html|title=Spieker Conic and generalization of Nagle line|last=de Villiers|first=M.|date=2007|website=Dynamic Mathematics Learning}}</ref> Also, the midpoints of each side of the medial triangle are found and connected to the midpoint of the opposite line through the Nagel point.<ref name=":3" /> Each of these lines share a common midpoint, S.<ref name=":3" /> With each of these lines reflected through S, the result is 6 points within the medial triangle. Draw a conic through any 5 of these reflected points and the conic will touch the final point.<ref name=":05" /> This was proven by de Villiers in 2006.<ref name=":05" />

== Spieker radical circle ==
The Spieker [[Power center (geometry)|radical circle]] is the circle, centered at the Spieker center, which is orthogonal to the three [[Incircle and excircles of a triangle|excircles]] of the medial triangle.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/ExcirclesRadicalCircle.html|title=Excircles Radical Circle|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|website=MathWorld- A Wolfram Web Resource}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/RadicalCircle.html|title=Radical Circle|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|website=MathWorld- A Wolfram Web Resource}}</ref>
